title: Convert character <--> date
description:
If an Excel file has a date as a column name, it gets converted to a character string containing an integer. For example, `2015-07-27` is converted to `"42212"`.

I put an example at [this gist](https://gist.github.com/kbroman/6b4ebcabc054d9cee9d6).

title: Blank cells are read as NA even when asked not to
description:
`read_excel` is still treating empty cells as `NA` when `""` is removed from the `na` argument:

```r
path <- readxl_example("geometry.xlsx")
read_excel(path, range="B1:D6", col_names=c("B", "C", "D"), na=character(0))
```

```
# A tibble: 6 x 3
  B     C     D    
  <chr> <chr> <chr>
1 NA    NA    NA   
2 NA    NA    NA   
3 B3    C3    D3   
4 B4    C4    D4   
5 B5    C5    D5   
6 B6    C6    D6 
```

This is the expected output:

```
# A tibble: 6 x 3
  B     C     D    
  <chr> <chr> <chr>
1 ""    ""    ""   
2 ""    ""    ""   
3 B3    C3    D3   
4 B4    C4    D4   
5 B5    C5    D5   
6 B6    C6    D6   
```

title: reading a series of empty cells returns a 0x0 tibble, rather than an MxN table of NA values
description:
Consider reading a blank Excel spreadsheet:
```
read_excel("blank.xlsx", "Sheet1", "A1:C1", na = "", col_names = FALSE)
# A tibble: 0 x 0
```
I would expect this to instead return a 1x3 tibble of `NA` values.

title: Drop our bounds-sanitizer workaround
description:
Once I re-vendor libxls 1.6.4, the workaround from #771 can be basically be removed.

[A recent libxls commit](https://github.com/libxls/libxls/commit/e78934c3f240b2e0da1f3c5cee8b2f6b7089a58d), made in response to [an issue about GCC 14's `-fsanitize=bounds-strict` errors](https://github.com/libxls/libxls/issues/144), restores C99 flexible array members for the variable-length record structs (`MULRK`, `MULBLANK`, `LABEL`, etc.) when compiled as C, keeping `[1]` only under C++ via a new `XLS_FLEXIBLE_ARRAY` macro. libxls had [switched them all to `[1]` in 2018](https://github.com/libxls/libxls/commit/b3fed3cc6763fe07f276ad487bd87ce22732e8d2) for C++ compatibility, prompted by [a readxl-motivated issue](https://github.com/libxls/libxls/issues/15). The new commit fixes the sanitizer errors at the source, so readxl's local workaround from [the sanitizer-fix PR](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/pull/771) is no longer needed.

There appear to be two open issues at 
- https://github.com/libxls/libxls/issues/155
- https://github.com/libxls/libxls/issues/156

dating back to January, with no apparent follow-up.  Someone needs to sit down and address this, the issue reports / CVEs do not offer patches but seem to offer hints. 

This issue is a courtesy requested in the thread referenced above.  Probably easiest to follow-up here.

title: Support for multi-value cells
description:
A few days ago [Microsoft announced](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoft365insiderblog/put-multiple-values-in-one-cell-with-lists-and-arrays-in-excel/4559395) that Excel cells now accept lists, arrays, and nested arrays in a single cell. These changes are available in a Beta version preview at this time, so no immediate changes are required or recommended, but scoping out support in advance might be nice.

### Current state

`read_xlsx()` [accepts `"list"` as a `col_type`](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/main/R/read_excel.R#L382) and [produces a single vector](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/main/src/SheetView.h#L258:L284): 

> A list cell loads a column as a list of length 1 vectors, which are typed using the type guessing logic from `col_types = NULL`, but on a cell-by-cell basis.

`xl/metadata.xml` and the `xl/richData/` directory [are not considered](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/main/src/XlsxWorkBook.h#L243:L353) as part of XLSX parsing as `xl/sharedStrings.xml` or `xl/styles.xml` are. 

[The `vm` (value metadata index)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/documentformat.openxml.spreadsheet.cell?view=openxml-3.0.1#remarks) attribute on a cell [is not considered](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/main/src/XlsxCell.h#L9:L14) in the same way `s` (style index) or `t` are (cell data type).

### Investigate support for

- 1D homogenous array or list (e.g. `{"dog";"cat";"turtle";"duck"}`)
- 1D heterogenous array or list (e.g. `{"dog";15.3;09/24/2026}`)
- 2D heterogenous array (e.g. `{{"cat";11.1;03/26/2022};{"dog";15.3;09/24/2026};{"turtle";27.9;02/15/2013}}`) 
- 2D homogenous array (e.g. `{{"cat";"dog";"turtle"};{"house";"shed";"patio"}}`)
- key:value pairs within any of the above (e.g. `{"dog:brown";"cat:orange";"turtle:green"}`)

Example XLSX files covering each of the above scenarios could be drafted, unzipped, and inspected to determine proper parsing route and what R data type is most appropriate.

description:

I have a data set in Excel I'm try to import into R. The file opens without issue. The data starts on the 6th line and I only wanted to import a part of the file so I did:
```
library(readxl)
read_excel("myfile.xslx", range = "A7:P100")
```
I immediately get this screen:
![R crash](https://imgur.com/VXYwOWn.png)

# Reprex
After [downloading the file](https://filedropper.com/d/s/0B3oelp1L1IXYqqUiRWaZDDqMvGiKP) simply do:
```
readxl::read_excel(file, range = "A7:P100")
```
where `file` is the path.
# Expected behavior
1. No session crash
2. Get the data in the A7:P100 range imported into R

title: Declaration of int64_t causes failure on Alpine
"readxl Workflows" vignette has a minor issue when checking for equality
description:
The check that ensures equality between the original Excel spreadsheet and the CSV snapshot fails in the [vignette("readxl-workflows")](https://readxl.tidyverse.org/articles/readxl-workflows.html#cache-a-csv-snapshot) article.  The check can be found [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/main/vignettes/articles/readxl-workflows.Rmd#L70) in the R markdown file.

My guess is that it's because the object classes are different and the `problems` attribute that `readr` seems to be adding.
```r
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

iris_xl <- readxl_example("datasets.xlsx") %>% 
  read_excel(sheet = "iris") %>% 
  write_csv("iris-raw.csv")

iris_xl
dir(pattern = "iris")

iris_alt <- read_csv("iris-raw.csv")
## readr leaves a note-to-self in `spec` that records its column guessing,
## so we remove that attribute before the check
attr(iris_alt, "spec") <- NULL
identical(iris_xl, iris_alt)
```
What would be the "right" way to make the call to `base::identical()` return `TRUE`? Calling `as_tibble()` on the `iris_alt` object before comparing them works, but maybe this is a bad idea? 
```r
identical(iris_xl, as_tibble(iris_alt))
```
Alternatively, I can follow the approach in the vignette by first removing the `problems` attribute. Then I can set the `class` of the `iris_alt` object equal to that of `iris_xl`.
```r
attr(iris_alt, "problems") <- NULL
attr(iris_alt, "class") <- class(iris_xl)
identical(iris_xl, iris_alt)
```
In my view an easy  solution is to call `base::all.equal()` with `check.attributes = FALSE`.  Even easier is to use (the now deprecated) `dplyr::all_equal()`.
```r
all.equal(iris_xl, iris_alt, check.attributes = FALSE)
all_equal(iris_alt, iris_xl)
```
The question is if it's important that the check fails if the objects have differing attributes? There might exist scenarios where differing attributes between the original Excel spreadsheet and the CSV file can cause problems down the road?

title: Access is denied warning on valid paths that get read successfully
description:
When reading Excel files on a network drive without access to the underlying folder, the file is read correctly, however, a warning with the text _Access is denied_ is generated.

This is likely due to the path being processed using `normalizePath`  without `mustwork = FALSE` , and it is documented that `normalizePath`  may throw these errors when it cannot access the underlying directories, even when the path is valid and the user has access to the file.

``` r
setwd("\\\\some/network/path")
openxlsx::write.xlsx(data.frame(a = 1), "example.xlsx")
readxl::read_xlsx("example.xlsx")
#> Warning in normalizePath(path.expand(path), winslash, mustWork):
#> path[1]="example.xlsx": Access is denied
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>       a
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     1
```

title: Unable to Import or Retrieve Excel Data
description:
I’m using Posit Cloud for my coursework and am experiencing repeated crashes when trying to upload and import a large Excel file (the BRFSS dataset).

Here’s what’s happening:

I successfully upload the Excel file to my project.

When I click “Import Dataset” and select the BRFSS file, the system starts to load, but then logs me out or restarts my session.

I’ve been able to upload and import smaller files without issues.

This behavior occurs even when I try in a new project.

I’ve confirmed the file is in my project directory and tried different browsers. I also used the downloaded R Studio, but my MacBook seems incompatible and will not allow me to retrieve the data when coding.

My goal is to work with the full BRFSS dataset in RStudio Cloud. I’m comfortable using R code directly, but I need to know if there’s a way to increase my memory limit or a recommended method for importing large files without crashing the session.

title: Ignore hidden rows or columns
description:
## Requested Feature
Excel is able to hide rows. This can be done manually by the user from excel, but this can also be automatically imposed by an Autofilter set by the user. It would be nice if this package allows an optional argument that ignores any hidden rows/columns from being loaded in the data frame. The default behaviour should be that all rows are read, just as is the case in the current version of openxlsx. By toggling the optional argument it would be possible to ignore the hidden rows/columns.

Would it be possible to implement such a feature?

title: Better error message when Excel file is open (Windows?)
description:
It's possible that this issue has been solved in a newer release, and/or that this is Windows-specific. But, I would love a more helpful error message when trying to load a file that is also open in Excel. Here's the current error message I get:

```
Error in utils::unzip(zip_path, list = TRUE) : 
  zip file 'C:\Users\[long file path]\SpreadsheetName.xlsx' cannot be opened
```

This feels ripe for a `tidyverse` helpful error message, like perhaps 

```
Error in utils::unzip(zip_path, list = TRUE) : 
  zip file 'C:\Users\[long file path]\SpreadsheetName.xlsx' cannot be opened
Do you have the Excel file open in another program? Try closing the spreadsheet everywhere else and running your code again. 
```

title: Support reading from more general inputs
description:
Right now readxl reads only from xlsx and xls files.

In the fullness of time, some functionality for supporting more general inputs will be pulled out of readr, at which point readxl can exploit that. We might implement an interim solution for some of these in the meantime.

This issue will cover all related feature requests (all of which I'm now closing):

  * #192 input via rawConnection
  * #183 URL support?
  * #115 align all read_* decompression and download behavior with read_delim()
  * #93 Read file directly from memory
  * #518 Feature Request: ability to read from HDFS

title: Error when running `excel_sheets()` on file whose name includes "zip"
description:
Encountered this issue when trying to read a file wherein the name includes, "zip" (referring to US ZIP codes). The file itself is not a compressed file, but an Excel workbook with multiple sheets. The error message reads,
```
Error in utils::unzip(zip_path, list = TRUE) : 
  zip file '<filename_that_includes_zip>.xlsx' cannot be opened

title: Warning seen with sanitizers
description:
Collecting various links and snippets to make this easier for me to analyze.

Now that v1.4.4 is on CRAN, there is a new deadline to address this issue: "Please correct before 2025-03-14 to safely retain your package on CRAN."

---

gcc-UBSAN result from CRAN's additional issues, pertaining to readxl v1.4.3

https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/bdr/memtests/gcc-UBSAN/readxl/

title: Mixed boolean and numeric values in a column causes read_excel to crash Rstudio but works fine from command line
description:
I was having a ton of problems with read_excel crashing my Rstudio session. I googled around, tried the suggested methods of re-saving the excel in different tools, formats, or OS. Nothing worked.

Then, I tried to make a silly test in an Rscript to run it from the command line, to see if I got some additional output, and it simply worked flawlessly without crashing. From there, I found out that the culprit is having a mix of boolean and numeric values in the same column. Opening such excel crashes Rstudio, but works from command line giving a few warnings.

Might this help explain previous issues with these crashes?

---

Brief description of the problem

```r
library(readxl)

# basedir<-"wherever/your/files/are"

file_crash <- file.path(basedir,"repexp_column_mixed.xlsx")
data <- readxl::read_excel(path = file_crash, 
                           sheet = "Sheet1",
                           col_names = F, 
                           trim_ws = T)
warnings()
dim(data)


file_noCrash <- file.path(basedir,"repexp_column_toNumber.xlsx")
data <- readxl::read_excel(path = file_noCrash, 
                           sheet = "Sheet1",
                           col_names = F, 
                           trim_ws = T)
warnings()
dim(data)

```

Running the "crash" chunk crashes Rstudio and gives this output in command line:

```
New names:
• `` -> `...1`
• `` -> `...2`
• `` -> `...3`
Warning messages:
1: Coercing boolean to numeric in C1 / R1C3
2: Coercing boolean to numeric in C3 / R3C3
3: Coercing boolean to numeric in C5 / R5C3
4: Coercing boolean to numeric in C7 / R7C3
[1] 7 3
```

Running the "non-crash" chunk works fine in Rstudio and gives this output in command line:

```
New names:
• `` -> `...1`
• `` -> `...2`
• `` -> `...3`
[1] 7 3
```

title: read_excel() Ignores Columns if Empty Until Around Line 1000
description:
When using read_excel() to read an Excel file, I noticed that columns are ignored if they remain empty until approximately line 1000. This behavior disappears when explicitly setting col_types. However, I couldn’t find any mention of this behavior in the readxl documentation, specifically for the read_excel() function. So, I’m unsure whether this is an expected limitation or a bug.

Some time ago, I believe I encountered a similar issue, but it happened around line 800, and instead of ignoring the column, it was converting values into boolean.

````r
setwd("")
library(readxl)

dados <- read_excel("test.xlsx") # does not read after line 1000
dados2 <- read_excel("test.xlsx", col_types = c("text", "text")) # this works

print(dados[997:1005, ]) # didn't get the values from the sheet (var2)
print(dados2[997:1005, ]) # it captured the values from the sheet (var2)

````

title: Number >1 converted to boolean TRUE without any warning
description:
In the following example, readxl returns TRUE instead of 599, without any warnings nor errors.

This doesn't happen with xlsx, openxlsx or openxlsx2.

I understand this is related to readxl guessing the column type using the first 1000 rows, but it should return at least a warning if not an error if the data it encounters is incompatible with the column type it guessed.

[test.xlsx](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/16726813/test.xlsx)

```r
indf <- readxl::read_xlsx("test.xlsx")
indf %>% filter(project_id==1001) %>% pull("budget")
# returns TRUE
# should return 599
```

title: Have to manually open certain xls files in Excel with RStudio running in order for read_excel to work
description:
Hello, I've encountered an issue with **read_excel** function with certain xls files I received. I need to open RStudio, then separately open and close each xls file in Excel before read_excel will function properly. If I do not, it creates an object but with 0 obs 8 x 0 columns. 

I don't know how these files were originally created and if they had any special properties but the cause may be because they were shared via the accellion secure file transfer platform (https://www.accellion.com/platform/simple/secure-file-sharing/)  Any ideas as to what could be causing this, and why the opening of the file in Excel--even if I don't make any edits or change filetype--resolves it?

Read excel is working fine for me otherwise, including on other xls (MS Excel 1997-2003) files even after I perform multiple steps of downloading, compressing, emailing, extracting, etc.

title: option to repeat value in merged cells
description:
Moving discussion from: https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/pull/220#issuecomment-298394447

Currently (I think) merged cells are handled by placing the value in the left-top cell of the range and placing NA in all other cells. Makes sense in many situations.

Another useful option might be to repeat the value across the previously merged range. That would, for example, be helpful in tidying files with multiple headers, as detailed here: https://howisonlab.github.io/datawrangling/Handling_multi_indexes.html#a-tidyverse-solution

However, with your suggestions from the other thread, tidyr::fill works for this sensibly if one does a little transposing:

```R
# read, fill, and collapse 4 rows of multiple headers from merged cells
headers <- read_excel(filename, col_names = FALSE, na="..", n_max = 4)
# fill only works down or up, so have to transpose headers
long_headers = data.frame(t(headers))
long_headers <- fill(long_headers,1:4) # all four columns
headers <- data.frame(t(long_headers)) # back to vertical.
```

Nonetheless, an option to unmerge and fill all cells might still be useful.

title: col_types = 'text_as_shown' ?
description:
This is related to #462 (closed)

I understand why it was closed but I'd like to make the case for a 'text_as_shown' option for column types.

In many cases what is shown in excel is not the truth, so we're better off taking the actual value rather than what is shown.

In my case I have on one hand a lookup table in R that I don't create, which contains a column with "66.67%" stored as text (this column can also store actual text), and a value to look up, and on the other hand an excel file with this "66.67%" value typed by the user, expecting it to work with the lookup.

This will be read by read_excel() as "0.6....67" if I read it as text, and in order to to the lookup I have to do some awkward data wrangling. 

Granted, I realise the design is not great, but I'm not responsible for it and this will be easily simplified if I could specify `"text_as_shown"` as a value to `col_types`, it would also be explicit enough so that I don't believe users would import wrong data by mistake more than they would without this option.

title: Feature request: factors in col_types
description: I would like to request that the `col_types` argument of `read_excel()` and related functions allow specifying factor as a column type. This is especially relevant for columns that are automatically guessed to be numeric but that I would like to treat as factors (e.g., numerical IDs of experimental blocks). Of course it is possible to coerce those columns to factor in a later step, but it would be helpful if it were possible to do this within `read_excel()`.

title: Force col_types for vector of known columns, default guess for other columns
description:
Reading a mutable xlsx when you know few of the columns names, it would be great to call `col_types` as `cols` function, using
```r
col_types = cols(.default = "?",  known_mixed_column = "c")
```
This approach is used in `readr::read_csv2`, and brings great functionality, that is not confused with `guess_max = n_max`, when I want to force types.
Current implementation of `coltypes` requires either NULL to guess all from the spreadsheet or a character vector containing one entry per column from these options: "skip", "guess", "logical", "numeric", "date", "text" or "list".
This approach is not possible when you still don't know the whole spreadsheet content.

title: FR: Check Excel sheets and consistency with readr
description:
Hi,

I was wondering if it would be possible to add a check for Excel sheets?

When I miswrite the Excel sheet, I have to go investigate the Excel file, but I wrote a small helper to help for that with `rlang::arg_match()` that gives helpful error message.

Also, would it be possible to rename the `path` argument to `file`, just like in readr, and `.name_repair` to `name_repair` since all other arguments in `read_excel()`  don't start with `.`.

Thanks
``` r
library(readxl)

read_excel(readxl_example("datasets.xlsx"), sheet = "iris2")
#> Error: Sheet 'iris2' not found


# Helper with consistency with readr
read_excel_check <- function(file, sheet = NULL, name_repair = "unique") {
  if (!is.null(sheet) && rlang::is_string(sheet)) {
      all_sheets <- readxl::excel_sheets(path = path)
      rlang::arg_match(sheet, all_sheets)
    }

  read_excel(
    path = file,
    sheet = sheet,
    .name_repair = name_repair
  )
}
read_excel_check(
  readxl_example("datasets.xlsx"),
  sheet = "iris2",
  name_repair = "universal"
  )
#> Error in `read_excel_check()`:
#> ! `sheet` must be one of "iris", "mtcars", "chickwts", or "quakes", not
#>   "iris2".
#> ℹ Did you mean "iris"?
```

<sup>Created on 2023-04-14 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Edit: This addition is costly in terms of performance. For a small datasets, it increases computing time by ~30%, but it reduces when the data is larger, and only check is `sheet` is not `NULL`

```r

title: Problems reading files with Windows path containing special characters
description:
Please briefly describe your problem and what output you expect. If you have a question, please don't use this form. Instead, ask on <https://stackoverflow.com/> or <https://community.rstudio.com/>.

Please include a minimal reproducible example (AKA a reprex). If you've never heard of a [reprex](http://reprex.tidyverse.org/) before, start by reading <https://www.tidyverse.org/help/#reprex>.

---

Brief description of the problem
I have always read Excel files into RStudio using read_excel(). My data files are stored inside a company OneDrive account and the path includes the name of the company. The issue only appeared recently. 

This is the error message I get: 

Error in file.exists(path) : 
  file name conversion problem -- name too long?

I think the issue is that the company name contains an unusual character, the Norwegian character ("ø"). If I move the Excel file to another location, e.g. "C:/Users/jansun/test folder" it loads without any problem. 
As soon as I add the "ø" character in the folder name, it returns the same error message. 
The same applies to the other specifically Norwegian characters "æ" and "å". 
I think the issue is related to R or Windows' handling of unusual characters, unfortunately I don't have a Mac or Linux install to test this hypothesis. 


```r
library(readxl)
colour <- read_excel(path = "C:/Users/jansun/OneDrive - Møreforsking AS/R/SAFERIMTA/data/Colour analysis SAFERIMTA.xlsx", 
                                        sheet = "til R")
```
Error message: 
Error in file.exists(path) : 
  file name conversion problem -- name too long?

description:

using httr's GET.

But when I try to read this file, using:

myasset <- "iShares-Core-SP-500-UCITS-ETF-USD-Acc_fund"
read_excel(paste(my_wd, myasset, ".xls", sep=""), sheet = "Holdings")

I get the error message: 

Error: 
  filepath: [mywd]\iShares-Core-SP-500-UCITS-ETF-USD-Acc_fund.xls

When I manually open the file, and I go to "Save as", I see that even though the file is saved as "*.xls", the extension is ".xml". I have checked with Blackrock, the provider, and also they see ".xml".

Is there an R way to do that automatically?

title: Use Excel column names or RC reference as default names in read_excel
description:
Reading in an excel range with `col_names = FALSE` results in uninformative name creation messages:

```r
d = read_excel(my_book, my_sheet, "A1:C6", col_names = FALSE)

#> New names:
#> • `` -> `...1`
#> • `` -> `...2`
#> • `` -> `...3`
```
Neither the message or the resulting names are helpful or clear. However, it should be simple to derive appropriate default names from the workbook columns and/or RC notation, both of which result in valid names:

- A1:C6 --> "A", "B", "C"
- R1C1:R6C3 --> "C1", "C2", "C3"

You could also generate default row names using this logic.

title: Allow user to specify col type is just date or time (vs full datetime)
description:
https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/5fbe9975d3afb97224332489f05d6688974e79a8/src/ColSpec.h#L129-L134

In the above lines of code, the numFmt values, in most cases, specify dates without times.  For example:
* numFmtId 14: mm-dd-yy only has date components, and numFmtId 15 as well
* 16 and 17 are imprecise dates without all components (16 is missing year; 17 is missing day)
* 18-21 are time-only formats with no dates
* 22 is a date-time

All of the above, and their equivalents in other languages, should be returned to the R user with the correct date precision.

For the formats that do not include times, they should be returned as a class `Date` object while formats that do include times should return as a class `POSIXct` object.  Returning everything as a `POSIXct` object gives an inaccurate picture of the precision.

Returning more than what is visually presented (especially the time-only formats showing as being on the day 1899-12-31) misrepresents the available data.

The representation of more data than are provided is also related to tidyverse/lubridate#690.

title: Vignette with background and practical strategies re: datetimes and friends
description:
Many things in Excel are stored as serial dates but, due to their format, *look* like something else to a user, leading the user to believe we can actually import whatever they're eyeballs are seeing in the Excel interface.

Recent example:

https://twitter.com/TomSaundersNZ/status/1336081299354730497

> Quick #rstats question: I'm importing data with readxl, it contains elapsed time stored in excel as HH:MM:SS, but R displays as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS (due to excel). How do I tell R these are durations?

It's natural that many suggested workaround route through character, but there are better workarounds.

Here's one suggested by @Hadley for the specific challenge above:

```
as_duration <- function(x) {
  s <- difftime(x, as.POSIXct("1899-12-31"), type = "seconds")
  hms::hms(s)
}
```

It would be helpful to have a vignette explaining this problem to users, i.e. that what they see in Excel is, in general, NOT what's stored on disk and is often NOT literally available to readxl. It would also be a good place to collect recommended workarounds for specific situations.

Related to #118 and all of its many friends.

title: The 'd' in [red] is interpreted as a date format
description:
https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/0d9ad4f570f6580ff716e0e9ba5048447048e9f0/src/ColSpec.h#L145-L148

That was too tempting for [somebody](https://github.com/CAPITAmodel/CAPITA), who created this beauty (see `MedicareAndLevies!Q:Q` ):
* Original file: [CPS v17-09-12.xlsb.zip](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/1327822/CPS.v17-09-12.xlsb.zip)
* Converted to xlsx using Excel 2010: [CPS v17-09-12.xlsx](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/1327821/CPS.v17-09-12.xlsx)

How to fix?

https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/0d9ad4f570f6580ff716e0e9ba5048447048e9f0/src/ColSpec.h#L150

... like the [awful hack](https://github.com/nacnudus/tidyxl/blob/89a9e0dec1ef74affcfda6124fb75d6d9707328e/src/styles.cpp#L254-L267) in tidyxl? :wink:



```cpp
// Adapted from hadley/readxl
bool styles::isDateFormat(std::string formatCode) {
  for (size_t i = 0; i < formatCode.size(); ++i) {
    switch (formatCode[i]) {
      case 'd':
        // Might be as in "[Red]"
        if (i < formatCode.size() - 1) {
          // there's at least one more character
          if (formatCode[i+1] == ']') {
            break;
          } else {
            return true;
          }
        }
```

Reprex:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
#> Loading tidyverse: ggplot2
#> Loading tidyverse: tibble
#> Loading tidyverse: tidyr
#> Loading tidyverse: readr
#> Loading tidyverse: purrr
#> Loading tidyverse: dplyr
#> Conflicts with tidy packages ----------------------------------------------
#> filter(): dplyr, stats
#> lag():    dplyr, stats
library(readxl)

source_url <- "https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/1327821/CPS.v17-09-12.xlsx"
filename <- "CPS v17-09-12.xlsx"
sheetname <- "MedicareAndLevies"

download.file(source_url, filename, mode = "wb")

x <- read_xlsx(filename, sheetname, skip = 6)
class(x$MedLevSurRate2)
#> [1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt"
```

The culpable number formats:

```r
library(tidyxl)
y <- tidy_xlsx(filename, sheetname) # Slow. I wish I could call Jim Hester for advice.

numFmt <- tibble(numFmt = y$formats$local$numFmt,
                 id = seq_along(y$formats$local$numFmt))

y$data[[1]] %>%
  filter(row >= 8, col == 17) %>%
  left_join(numFmt, by = c("local_format_id" = "id")) %>%
  distinct(numeric, numFmt)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   numeric                               numFmt
#>     <dbl>                                <chr>
#> 1  0.0100     "#,##0.00_ ;[Red]\\-#,##0.00\\ "
#> 2  0.0125 "#,##0.0000_ ;[Red]\\-#,##0.0000\\ "
#> 3      NA                              General
```

title: readxl skips (and then later appends?) embedded blank lines

How can I help solve this problem? It appears to be pretty specific to this spreadsheet (I can't seem to come up with a generic example that causes the same problem) but I don't understand why.

```r

description:

FYI. This file comes from a french administration and is supposed to be a thesaurus of possible medical procedures. Main data is on the second sheet (first one is the data dictionary). title: Interplay between readxl spinner and cli progress bar
description:
Let  me apologise first because I am not including a reprex to showcase the problem but given that the issue has to do with dynamic output in R console I would not know how to make a static reprex to include here.

My case is that I am reading various XLSX files with `readxl::read_xlsx` and I am trying to track the progress with a progress bar from the R package `{cli}`. Note that I am trying to track the progress over these files, not the progress of reading one file --- as `readxl` does. I am basically setting a progress bar with `cli::cli_progress_bar`, then updating the bar with `cli::cli_progress_update`. The loop is being performed by `purrr::map_dfr`.

Essentially, the problem I am finding is that even when I turn off readxl spinner with the option `progress = FALSE` when calling `readxl::read_xlsx`, I still get the progress bar generated by `cli::cli_progress_bar` flushed (i.e. it disappears) between reads of the files.

The reason I think this has to do with `{readxl}` somehow interfering with console output is the fact that if I comment the `readxl::read_xlsx` call altogether and replace it with a simple `Sys.sleep(1)` call then I see the cli progress bar as intended.

title: Consider increasing type guessing length of column when all initially scanned data is NA
description:
I sometimes have excel spread sheets with sparse character data in some columns. For instance, the dataset might have a few thousand cases and there is a character variable that has some information at row 2000 or 5000, etc..

Perhaps this is a simple example. 

    x <- data.frame(x = seq(1:10000), y = c(rep(NA, 9000), rep("test", 1000)))

I'm not quite sure on the current default behavior of `read_excel`, but at least in one instance it has treated the variable as a logical. As a result, the character data is deleted.

I think that more effective behaviour would be to scan the variable for longer when the scanned data based on `guess_max` is `NA`.

I.e., if guess_max = 1000, and the first 1000 values of a variable are NA, then scan the remainder of the variable.

This would result in better variable typing and reduce data loss.

title: Enable reading directly from OneDrive/Sharepoint
description:
Would it be possible to enable to read directly from Excel files stored in **OneDrive/Sharepoint** in a **similar way** to what is possible with Google Sheets using **googlesheets4**?

Basically allowing the `path` argument in `read_excel()` to be the link to a OneDrive file, just like the `ss` argument of `read_sheet()` from googlesheets4. 

Example use case:
```r
df <- read_excel("https://my-sharepoint-site/documents/my-file.xlsx", sheet="sheet1")
```
I think this would make workflows involving OneDrive/Sharepoint easier to manage.

title: Change the default value of `sheet` to `1` instead of `NULL`
description:
Can the default value of the `sheet` argument in `read_excel_` (and derived functions) be `1` not `NULL`? Looking at the code for standardise_sheet, there is a line that says

```
if (is.null(sheet)) {
    sheet <- 1L
  }
```

It seems to me that having `sheet = 1L` in the function args would do the same thing. 

Obviously it works, so why change? Without going into great depth, if `sheet` is conditionally set, then I can't see a sensible way to set it to `NULL`. I can set it conditionally to `1` of course, but then given this is really the default behaviour why not just set it to that in the first place?

title: A read_excel variant or argument to read each excel column into a data frame column
description:
A curse of messy excel files is information stored in formatting.

An excel cell doesn't just have a value, it also has (or can have) : 
* a formula
* a fill color
* a font
* a font color
* a font size

And more, like border formatting, conditional formatting specifications, validation list specifications... but I believe the variables above are the one that we'd most want structured.

I believe all this info could be stored in data frame columns. We could have by default each column be a 6 column data frame containing value + variables above (if several fonts, colors, or sizes in a single cell, that'd be NA).   Then we would unpack as desired using *tidyr* or filter such as in the following :

    # read file, specify to include cell metadata
    xl_df <- read_excel(path, include_metadata = TRUE)
    #filter on red cells of variable `some_var`
    dplyr::filter(xl_df, some_var$color == "#FF0000")

Alternately these data frame columns wouldn't be provided if they are default, which would allow us to just unpack everything, and only have color columns for variables that do have some colored cells for instance.

Alternately again, `include_metadata` could be a vector of colnames to import as data frame columns. `include_metadata = c("var3", "var22")`

Alternately again again,  `include_metadata` could be a list of vectors enumerating the metadata to include.  `include_metadata = list(var3 = "fill",  var22 = c("color", "font"))`

title: Does not compile on Alpine Linux
Re-export writexl::write_excel()?
read_xlsx can't detect indentation applied via a format
description:
The XLSX format allows cells to be "indented", which is usually used to denote hierarchical data. See for example NSF data tables such as https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf19301/assets/data/tables/sed17-sr-tab015.xlsx

This indenting data is ignored by read_xlsx, making it difficult to capture the nestings.

```r
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)

download.file("https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf19301/assets/data/tables/sed17-sr-tab015.xlsx",
              destfile = "local.xlsx", mode = "wb")

read_xlsx("local.xlsx", skip = 3) %>% 
  select(1)
```
Those column labels don't reflect the category > subcategory > sub-subcategory structure of the data. (system isn't letting me upload graphic)

**Desired Behavior**
Have loaded data reflect indentation levels, possibly by prepending TAB or SPACE characters (which I recognize would conflict, if trim_ws = TRUE)

title: read_xlsx adding trailing 0s during numeric to character conversion
description:
I'm having a weird (and difficult to reproduce) problem when reading in mixed numeric data. 

I have an excel file (exported from QuestionPro, a survey site).

One of my columns starts with:
8 9 5 "Don't know"

If I read in the only the first 3 rows using n_max, I get a numeric vector. However, when I read 4 rows, I get unexpected output:
structure(c("8.0", "9.0", "5.0", "Don't know"), class = 'character')

I've tried to replicate the problem (or provide a reprex), but if I copy the data from the problematic file into a new excel spreadsheet for testing, it reads in normally. 

In fact, in the course of testing this, I found that simply saving a new copy of the excel file fixes the problem (and increased the file size from 156KB to 169KB). 

Perhaps this is more an excel problem than a read_xl problem, but it strikes me as unexpected that read_xl reads in data differently depending on whether excel has opened/saved the file or not. What is going on under the surface here?

title: read_excel triggers wrong warning for dates before 1899-12-30
description:
## Note

This is an issue mentioned previously in https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/issues/547 which is now here isolated for clarity.

## The issue
Reading an xlsx file with dates before ~1900 triggers the warning:

https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/5fbe9975d3afb97224332489f05d6688974e79a8/src/utils.h#L67

However, that warning only makes sense for a specific invalid date: 1900-02-29; and not for every single date before ~1900. Thus a new condition and warning needs to be written to deal with this case.

title: readxl not compatible with openxlsx
description:
Hi there,

`readxl` does not preserve the class of a dataframe saved with `openxslx` package. Since `readxl` does not create xlsx files, one must use a package like `openxlsx`. But since the latter also opens xlsx files and **does preserve class**, ones asks why `readxl` is needed at all. It would be better if `readxl` could preserve the class of created excel files.

```
# create dataframe
df <- data.frame("var" = c(seq(1,10)))
class(df) # results is "data.frame"
# Export as xlsx
library(openxlsx)
write.xlsx(df,"df.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
# Import as xlsx
library(readxl)
df <- read_excel("df.xlsx")
# Check class of imported object
class(df) # results is "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

```

That will be preceded by a release of the [usethis package](https://usethis.r-lib.org), which will gain some functionality around detecting and adapting to a renamed default branch. There will also be a blog post at the time of this `master` --> `main` change.

title: read_xlsx evaluates 1000 rows of a column and if "NA" for the first 1000, makes the rest "NA" whether "NA" or not
description:
I needed to import .XLS files, but could not so I saved them as .XLSX After importing and binding, I found out too much later that in the original import - an important field - that was mostly blank but had important information - was imported as all "NA" (The original datasets had many more columns and rows. I figured out, through trial and error, that read_xlsx evaluates about 1000 rows and if all of these are NA, then it writes the rest of the import as NA for that field.

I resolved this by saving the files as .csv and trying read_csv, which did not behave this way and correctly imported the data.

ma7 <- read_xlsx("https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/7009850/file_f.xlsx")
ma8 <- read_xlsx("https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/7009851/file_e.xlsx")

title: Look into Solaris
description:
I decided not to worry about this when merging libxls v1.6.2, as historically we have claimed that readxl did not work on Solaris due to endian-ness bugs in libxls. I think those bugs are gone now and indeed @jimhester has noted that the current version of readxl appears to be passing on Solaris (https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_readxl.html).

However the new problem is that libxls's new use of locales will require some attention to Solaris.

Heads up: This means this fix probably also needs to be re-introduced, but perhaps a `config.h` generated on the relevant platform will be correct from the start. https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/commit/ea4d9ae26af0d7de7b57440db09e9249ae184bb4

Here's the r-hub report:

* <https://builder.r-hub.io/status/readxl_1.3.1.9000.tar.gz-03a98af04f114c44ac3b9c91a780b386>

title: Documentation: "readxl Workflows" vignette
description:
Just a note re clarification of the [readxl Workflows vignette](https://readxl.tidyverse.org/articles/articles/readxl-workflows.html), section "Iterate over multiple worksheets in a workbook".

set_names() occurs in both {magrittr} and in {rlang}.  It is only the latter of these that works with the example:
```r
path <- readxl_example("datasets.xlsx")
path %>%
  excel_sheets() %>%
  set_names() %>%
  map(read_excel, path = path)
```

`rlang::set_names()` will give the expected output, but `magrittr::set_names()` gives the error:
```r
Error in magrittr::set_names(.) : 
  1 argument passed to 'names<-' which requires 2
```

So if {magrittr} is loaded, but not {rlang}, the example as given will not work.

Using R 4.1.0, tidyverse 1.3.1, rlang 0.4.11, magrittr 2.0.1.

title: readxl removes comma from a text column
description:
Problem: readxl removes comma from a text column


---

I am using readxl  to read in data from files generated from a multiplate reader (example attached).  The data itself is  in B55:O102 where column O contains metadata on the excitation and emission wave lengths and indicates the blank reading for the corresponding fluorescence.  Column O is the the one that is handled in a manner that is "Possibly" buggy in readxl.  

readxl() properly (and automatically) identifies column O as a character column.  What is "wonky" is that for those rows where there are just two wave length separated by a comma, readxl "does me the favor" of removing the comma separating the two  wave lengths, as if it thinks these rows are intended to be a single large number written in business format. Interestingly, it does not provide the same  "help" in those rows that include the word Blank.  Here I get the expected behavior and the comma is maintained.  Ultimately, I want to parse column O into a blank indicator and a pair of wave lengths.  The disappearing comma on some rows makes this less straight forward.

I would understand it "helping" if the column type were numeric, but it seems just plain wrong in this context where the column is character.  I think this behavior should be classified as a "bug" when the column type is character.

```r
# path will depend on local context
Plate9_1130Export <- read_excel("H:/PlateReader/20200807 -DyeTest/Plate9_1130Export.xlsx",
                                range = "B55:O102", col_names = FALSE)

title: Use a named col_type
description:
I am reading a bunch of files with several columns, in some files these columns are in the files and in some other they are not (but they always contain the same information). In total there are 74 column names but I have 13, 13, 35, 38, 38, 44, 44 and 52 columns in each file. 

read_xlsx is having a hard time guessing what type is each column. I would like to provide a named col_type such that if the column name is found it applies that type of data. Now I need to explore each file and look what type of data has each column and in which position in order to specify the type. 

Currently only the position of `col_type` sets the type of the column. This would mean silently remove the missing col_types if there aren't in the file being read.

As a mock example I would like to be able to do something like this:

```r
col_type <- c("Fecha" = "date", "count" = "numeric", "position" = "text")
# Files of two columns
read_xlsx(file1, col_type = col_type)
# Files of all three columns in different order than the first one
read_xlsx(file1, col_type = col_type)
```

Ideally the check of the type should be done before cleaning the names (I have some columns with duplicate column names).

```r
library(readxl)

read_xlsx("~/Downloads/reprex.xlsx", sheet = 1, range = cell_cols("J:M"), skip = 1)

  ...1  ...2  junk    ...4

title: Remove obsolete Excel files from package
description:
I am not sure whether if this warrants a response from you, the developers, but I am regurlarly encountering the following issue: Whenever I try to update `readxl` (or `tidyverse`) for that matter, the corporate firewall prevents me from doing so because the package contains outdated Excel files (for instance, `clippy.xls` in `/extdata`). 

The firewall prevents from getting the package via CRAN, Github and manual download. The only option I have left is to download the package on a private device and (illegally) transfer it via USB to my work pc. 

I am not sure which purpose including these files in the package has and how many others behind corporate firewalls encounter the same issue, so please feel free to close this as you see fit.

Thanks for a great package, anyways!

title: read_excel can't read from row >99999..
description:
`read_excel` can't read data from rows beyond 99999 and throws different, unclear, errors when you try to do this.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

# this is fine
x <- read_excel("test100k.xlsx", range="A1:A99999")

# this is not fine
x <- read_excel("test100k.xlsx", range="A1:A100000")

title: Build on GitHub Actions
description:
Enable [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/features/actions) for this project. You will need to install the development version of usethis (`remotes::install_dev("usethis")`. For more details see [GitHub Actions for R](https://github.com/r-lib/actions/tree/master/examples).

- [ ] run `usethis::use_github_actions_tidy()`
  - [ ] Add badges in your clipboard to [README.md](../blob/master/README.md)
    - If `README.Rmd` exists add badges to that instead and run `devtools::build_readme()`.
- [ ] look at existing [.travis.yml](../blob/master/.travis.yml) and see if there is extra logic that needs to be included.
  - If `.travis.yml` builds a pkgdown site 
    - [ ] run `usethis::use_github_action("pkgdown.yaml")`
    - [ ] ping @jimhester to add `DEPLOY_PAT` to the repository secrets. 
- [ ] look at existing [appveyor.yml](../blob/master/appveyor.yml) and see if there is extra logic from `.travis.yml` and `appveyor.yml` that needs to be included.
- [ ] modify [R-CMD-check.yaml](../blob/.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml) with extra logic if needed.
- [ ] ping @jimhester to add codecov.io token `CODECOV_TOKEN` to the repository secrets.

title: Failure to read key ID column
description:
---

Brief description of the problem: the data are six character IDs (OK to read as integer or numeric, but not OK to read as "0" (when column type set) or 0. Image from Libre Office Calc.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10198404/55541096-91ba5f80-56c4-11e9-8532-b24acbbbaf14.png)

```r
download.file("https://prezydent2015.pkw.gov.pl/wyniki_tura2.zip", file.path(td, "wyniki_tura2.zip"))
unzip(file.path(td, "wyniki_tura2.zip"), files="wyniki_tura2.xls", exdir=td)
wyn2 <- readxl::read_excel(file.path(td, "wyniki_tura2.xls"))

title: Collapse multiple rows of headers (feature request)
description:
I frequently receive Excel files that have "complex" headers, where there are multiple rows of cells encoding a single column name. Usually there's included units, labels, or additional metadata, but rarely can the extra rows be thrown away and only the first kept. Here's an example:


![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13338560/41261664-c03a658e-6daa-11e8-8fc1-0ba83fa80478.png)



- In the workflow below, the first attempt erroneously puts the metadata in the first row of the tibble. This incorrectly coerces the parser to guess that 4 columns are character, not numeric. Additionally, we lose the name of the 6th column, converted to `X__1`, and the second treatment column is coerced to `Trt__1`.
- The second attempt correctly parses the column types, but we lose the names on the first 5 columns, and keep only the metadata. Since there are multiple columns with the unit "grams", that's not enough to reconstruct the original headers.
- The third attempt is a flavor of the first, manually removing the metadata row and forcing a reparse. Again, this loses one of the column names, and confuses the two treatment columns.
- The fourth attempt is my current workflow: I read in the top few rows that I know contain both names and metadata, collapse them with `paste`, and unlist them to get a vector of column names. Then I read in the data part of the sheet separately and add the names.

My desire: an additional argument to `read_excel` that's like `row_collapse = 1:2`, telling it to do that. 

---

``` r
library(readxl)                                                             
library(dplyr)                                                              
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'

#>

file_path <- "https://github.com/brianwdavis/public/raw/master/example.xlsx"
                                                                            
download.file(file_path, "example.xlsx", mode = "wb")                       
                                                                            
read_excel("example.xlsx")                                                  
#> # A tibble: 7 x 6
#>   Trt      Trt__1   `Dry wt` `Fresh wt` Temp  X__1     
#>   <chr>    <chr>    <chr>    <chr>      <chr> <chr>    
#> 1 Factor 1 Factor 2 grams    grams      C     replicate
#> 2 a        d        3        5          20    1        
#> 3 a        d        5        10         22    2        
#> 4 a        e        8        15         21    3        
#> 5 b        e        4        9          30    1        
#> 6 b        f        6        11         31    2        
#> 7 b        f        2        4          32    3
read_excel("example.xlsx", skip = 1)                                        
#> # A tibble: 6 x 6
#>   `Factor 1` `Factor 2` grams grams__1     C replicate
#>   <chr>      <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 a          d              3        5    20         1
#> 2 a          d              5       10    22         2
#> 3 a          e              8       15    21         3
#> 4 b          e              4        9    30         1
#> 5 b          f              6       11    31         2
#> 6 b          f              2        4    32         3
                                                                            
                                                                            
                                                                            
read_excel("example.xlsx") %>%                                              
slice(-1) %>%                                                               
mutate_all(readr::parse_guess)                                              
#> # A tibble: 6 x 6
#>   Trt   Trt__1 `Dry wt` `Fresh wt`  Temp  X__1
#>   <chr> <chr>     <int>      <int> <int> <int>
#> 1 a     d             3          5    20     1
#> 2 a     d             5         10    22     2
#> 3 a     e             8         15    21     3
#> 4 b     e             4          9    30     1
#> 5 b     f             6         11    31     2
#> 6 b     f             2          4    32     3
                                                                            
                                                                            
nms <-                                                                      
read_excel("example.xlsx", range = cell_rows(1:2), col_names = F) %>%       
summarise_all(funs(paste(na.omit(.), collapse = "_"))) %>%                  
unlist()                                                                    
nms

#>   "Trt_Factor 1"   "Trt_Factor 2"   "Dry wt_grams" "Fresh wt_grams" 
#>             X__5             X__6

read_excel("example.xlsx", skip = 2) %>%

title: column type conversion warnings can be overwhelming
description:
Sometimes I come across very large Excel files (e.g., 35,000 rows, 100 columns) where numeric values are stored in Excel as "text" cells. If readxl guesses that these are in fact numeric columns or if the column type is specified explicitly to be numeric, readxl spits out tons of warning messages about type conversions. Reading the excel file takes virtually forever if the number of rows is larger than just a couple of thousands, and it also seems to bring RStudio to its limits. If reading the file is interrupted, there seems to be a memory leak because after a couple of failed and interrupted attempts the R session in RStudio gets incredibly slow. It does not help to add "suppressWarnings" and "suppressMessages". If the col_types are defined explicitly to be in line with the cell types defined in the Excel file, the readxl call returns after reasonable time and converting the columns of the data frame afterwords is also quick:

```
df <- read_excel(inputFile, col_types = "text")
numericCols <- c(17, 23, 24, 25 + 2*(0:18), 76)
df[, dnaNumericCols] <- sapply(dna[, dnaNumericCols], as.numeric)
```

This is a real issue for large files because readxl can only be used after making sure that the col_types are specified to be exactly in sync with the cell types in the Excel file. This is painful if the number of columns is in the hundreds.

title: Add support for .xlw
description:
While read_excel works on .xlsm (wonderful!!), it doesn't appear to support the legacy .xlw. It would be incredibly helpful to support that format too if possible, since some government datasets are still .xlw only.

Error in read_fun(path = path, sheet = sheet, limits = limits, shim = shim,  :

```

There are a bunch of .xlw datasets here that would be good for testing: https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/ohim/summary95/section4.html

title: "NA" in date-formatted column prevents read_excel from interpreting it as a date
description:
If there are "na" values in a date-formatted excel column, as in "NA" was typed as opposed to the cell being left blank, then readxl cannot interpret the column as a date. Forcing date with the `col_types` argument works, but leaves a ton of error messages. This isn't a huge deal since a few error messages isn't that bad, but it was tricky to troubleshoot because to me "NA" is not an obvious data entry error, and in a large spreadsheet the "NA" was hidden and it was hard to figure out why some columns were importing properly and others were not. Also, the imported character NA's look very similar to the real NA's in the RStudio View window and in the console output.

make an example excel file that looks like this:

whatever | date column | bla | bla
-- | -- | -- | --
a | 10/22/87 | 1 | w
b | 6/18/99 | 2 | x
c | NA | 3 | y
d |   | 4 | z

and read in like this:
```r
> read_excel("~/Desktop/readxl_bug_repex.xlsx")
# A tibble: 4 x 4
  whatever `date column`   bla bla__1
  <chr>    <chr>         <dbl> <chr> 
1 a        32072             1 w     
2 b        36329             2 x

title: read_excel returns number instead of date
description:
_As per @jennybc 's suggestion on `https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/issues/134#issuecomment-441487546` I'm creating a new thread for this issue._

---

**Problem**: read_excel() fails to recognise/return dates and is instead returning numbers followed by this warning:

> 50: In read_fun(path = path, sheet_i = sheet, limits = limits,  ... :
>   Expecting numeric in AC3 / R3C29: got a date

Download this simple excel file and put it in the same directory as the R code: [Readxl_Erroneous_Date_Reading.xlsx](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/2659643/Readxl_Erroneous_Date_Reading.xlsx). Then run the following code:
```r
library(readxl)
DatesDS <-
  read_excel("Readxl_Erroneous_Date_Reading.xlsx",
             "3000",
             range = cell_limits(c(1, 4), c(NA, NA)),
             col_names = FALSE)

print(DatesDS)
```

Now, I understand that this is probably because it recognises that most of the rows are actually comprised of integers.
I would think that in such a situation, since a column cannot be both a Date and an Int/Double simultaneously (we're not in the quantum world here), perhaps everything should be returned as a string (character) instead so that we can parse dates as dates and integers as integers.

title: Datetime missing a second strikes back
Option to Stop reading at first Empty Row
description:
As of now, I am not aware of any way to make `readxl::read_excel()` to stop reading rows when it meets a row that is empty (all cells at that particular row are empty)

This is, for instance, the default behaviour of `excel.link::xl.read.file()` and it helps a lot when people create different things on the same sheet, but you only want to capture the first one.

---

What happens now:

```r
readxl::read_excel("SpreadSheet.xlsx")
```
|Col1|Col2|
|-----|-----|
|1     |1     |
|2     |2     |
|       |       |
|f      |f      |
|g     |g     |

What I suggest as an option:
```r
readxl::read_excel(
  "SpreadSheet.xlsx",
  StopAtFirstEmptyLine = TRUE
)
```
|Col1|Col2|
|-----|-----|
|1     |1     |
|2     |2     |

What I do now is:
```r
  MyDF <- readxl::read_excel("SpreadSheet.xlsx")

  FirstEmptyRow <- NA
  tmpDFBool <- sapply(MyDF, function(x) is.na(x) | is.null(x))
  for (i in 1:NROW(tmpDFBool)) {
    if (all(tmpDFBool[i, ]) == TRUE) {
      FirstEmptyRow <- i - 1
      break
    }
  }

  if (!is.na(FirstEmptyRow)) MyDF <- MyDF[1:FirstEmptyRow,]
```

So instead of reading less than the whole excel sheet, now the whole excel sheet is returned, then I apply a function to the whole sheet again, and then I return a new object which is a subset of the original.
So complexity-wise it went from `<n` to something like `2n + c`

title: Issue when using col_names, col_types, skip and missing values
description:
Update: other search incantations turned up #157, which is actually what I think this is most closely related to.

---

#81 and #137 are similar, but I don't think they are the same as this.

---

I'm reading in a large excel file in wide format and ran into an issue. I have recreated an example which I *think* boils down to these characteristics.

- the final columns are in the form `var_1`, `var_2`, ..., `var_50`, many of which are empty. In my example, I figured out that if you don't have a value in a column until row 1002, `read_excel` will treat them as logical. Thus, without specifying `col_types`, you get:

```
1: In read_fun(path = enc2native(normalizePath(path)), sheet_i = sheet,  ... :
  Expecting logical in AS1969 / R1969C45: got 'foo'
```

- while not stated in [the documentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/readxl/versions/0.1.1/topics/read_excel), unless I'm missing it, `col_names` should require `skip=1` if you want to specify your own header even though the data has it's own.

- now, to the issue: if you have a big data set and use `n_max` *and* you have a column with missing data in rows `>n` *and* use `skip=1` *and* specify your own `col_types`, you'll get an error like this:

```
Error: Sheet 1 has 49 columns, but `col_types` has length 70.
```

Here is [an excel file](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/3786815/col_name_col_type.xlsx) that reproduces this.
```
library(readxl)
data <- read_excel("~/Desktop/col_name_col_type.xlsx",
                   skip=1,
                   col_names=c("foo", "bar", paste0("x", 1:3)),
                   col_types=rep("text", 5), n_max=50)
Error: Sheet 1 has 4 columns, but `col_types` has length 5.
```

In my case, this resolved once I removed my troubleshooting `n_max` option. I *think* the issue happens because `skip=1` removes the first row, which was the only row containing any text in these far out columns. In addition, in rows `<n_max`, these values were also missing. Something about specifying `col_types` for these columns in which it can't find any values seems to cause the issue.

Possible proposal: for columns in which `col_names` or `col_types` are specified... populate `NA` and perhaps issue a simple warning? In many cases, this is probably a mismatch of lengths (warnings/errors already occur when we find more columns than provided names/types), but in other cases, it might be that the user wants to specify names/types and the columns are empty, or empty in current rows, but not all of them.

    read_excel('.xlsx-file', trim_ws=F)

    ## doesn't work, whitespace is always trimmed
    read_xls('.xls-file', trim_ws=F)

    ## doesn't work, whitespace is trimmed regardless.
    read_xlsx('.xlsx-file', trim_ws=F)

It's obvious that the misbehaviour is either a documentation problem (are `read_xls` and `read_xlsx` meant to have a `trim_ws` parameter?) or a code problem when calling the `read_excel_` wrapper (the `trim_ws` parameter is not passed along at all).

title: col_types and col_names
description:
I get an error message "Error: Element 1 has length 2, not 1 or 12" when specifying col_types and col_names for read_excel, even though my specified types are length 12.

I am using publicly available data. The following code downloads the data, though you will need to change the destination (tourism.path).

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(readxl)

tourism.path <- "T:/TIGR_EFP/REVENUE AND TAXATION/DATABASES/Tourism"
domestic.url <- "https://www.business.vic.gov.au/tourism-industry-resources/research/domestic-and-regional-research"
international.url <- "https://www.business.vic.gov.au/tourism-industry-resources/research/international-research"

# Get xls data from tourism victoria
xls.tbl <- # Read urls from vcglr.url
             bind_rows(domestic.url %>% 
                       read_html()  %>%
                       rvest::html_nodes(., xpath=".//a[contains(@href, 'xls')]") %>% 
                       rvest::html_attr("href") %>%
                       # Add prefix and convet to a tibble
                       enframe(name=NULL, value = "urls"),
                       international.url %>% 
                       read_html()  %>%
                       rvest::html_nodes(., xpath=".//a[contains(@href, 'xls')]") %>% 
                       rvest::html_attr("href") %>%
                       # Add prefix and convet to a tibble
                       enframe(name=NULL, value = "urls")) %>%
             # Extract workbook name as variable downloads
             mutate(downloads=file.path(tourism.path,gsub(".*/","",urls))) %>%
             # Download files
             mutate(df=map2(urls, downloads, function(u,d) if(!file.exists(d)) download.file(u,d,mode="wb"))) %>%
             select(-df) %>%
             # Exract sheet names and unnest into tibble with all sheets to be dowloaded
             mutate(sheets=map(downloads, excel_sheets)) %>% 
             unnest() %>%
             filter(grepl("Domestic visitors to regions|Visitors & Nights Regional Vic",sheets))

tourism.names <- c("variable",2009:2019 %>% paste0("year_",.))
tourism.cols <- c("text",rep("numeric",11))

# Create tbl of visitor data based on xls.tbl above.
tourism.tbl <-  pmap_df(list(xls.tbl$downloads,
                            xls.tbl$sheets,
                            col_types=tourism.cols,
                            #col_names=tourism.names,
                            range="a4:l100"),
                       read_excel)
```

title: Write to .xlsx
description: We are currently using [openxlsx](https://github.com/awalker89/openxlsx) in [rio](https://github.com/leeper/rio). It offers read/write to .xlsx. [We'd like to incorporate reading from .xls (and thus import readxl)](https://github.com/leeper/rio/issues/19), but we don't want to lose write to .xlsx support. Any chance you can add write to .xlsx (ala what is available in openxlsx)? I don't think it make sense for us to import two different Excel-related packages.

title: Won't read non-lowercase .XLSX or .xlsm files
description:
Looks like the code for identifying the file type is being case-sensitive with extensions, so it will open `.xlsx` files but not `.XLSX`. 

```
> read_excel("epoch-1900.XLSX")
Error: Don't know how to parse extension XLSX
```

Since the extension-based file type detection on platforms Excel runs on is typically case-insensitive, it seems like `read_excel` should be too, with respect to detecting file formats.

It won't read `.xlsm` files, either. They're the same format as `.xlsx`, just with macros enabled.

```
> read_excel("with-macro.xlsm")
Error: Don't know how to parse extension xlsm
```

title: Controlling output of read_excel()
description:
Once you give user control of cell specification (#8), the next question will be if user can control the form of the output. I suspect right now it is always a `tbl_df` with default to a `stringsAsFactors = FALSE` mentality?

Re: header row, will you stick with `col_names =` instead of the more `read-table`-y `header = TRUE/FALSE`? Of course, what you've done with `col_names =` is more powerful.

What about dropping dimensions and returning (named) atomic vector instead of `tbl_df`?

I ask because, as in #8, I'd like to be a consistent as possible in gspreadr.

title: Rounding error when numbers are interpreted as characters
description:
If I create a simple Excel worksheet like

| col1 |
| --- |
| 73.1 |

`read_excel('minimal.xlsx')`

works as expected, interpreting col1 as type _num_ and the value as _73.1_

But if I then add a character value "x" in the next row like this

| col1 |
| --- |
| 73.1 |
| x |

now col1 is interpreted as type _char_ but the value changes to _73.099999999999994_

The strange rounding happens to some numbers but not others.

I'm using Excel 2010 on 32-bit Windows 7 and readxl 0.0.0.9000

title: Cells with partial colouring read the first colour chunk?
description:
I have an excel sheet with a cell containing "H2395" where the "H" is in red, and the "2395" is in black.

On reading in, this reads as "H" and drops the number.  This file for example:

https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/41868071/Results%20Plate%20SF325.xlsx

(On a sidenote, is it possible to retrieve the colour of a cell entry at all?  I have a bunch of sheets where (unfortunately) someone decided to store data based on the colour of the text in the cell...  Just "colour of first text" would do the trick.)

title: check.names default (and reading from URL)
description:
Great package. Two minor issues:

1) Can we add a check.names option (set to FALSE as default) for read_excel? Multi-word column names are currently being read "as is" from Excel, rather than having spaces replaced with periods.

2) I may have missed something, but is it possible to read .xls files directly from a URL?

title: Warning "unkown type 'inlineStr' leads to NA column with NA header
description:
In a larger excel sheet there is one tab that results in an additional column with NA as a header. A function like dplyr::distinct will fail on this column later. A warning for each row in the excel sheet is generated:

```
Warning messages:
1: In read_xlsx_(path, sheet, col_names = col_names, col_types = col_types,  ... :
  [3, 4]: unknown type 'inlineStr'
2: In read_xlsx_(path, sheet, col_names = col_names, col_types = col_types,  ... :
  [4, 4]: unknown type 'inlineStr'
3: In read_xlsx_(path, sheet, col_names = col_names, col_types = col_types,  ... :
```

It may have something to do with working in both Microsoft Excel and LibreOffice with the same document. There are references to similar issues in the [python-excel](https://github.com/python-excel/xlrd/issues/81) project, and a description of the conflicting xml [here](http://our.componentone.com/groups/topic/read-generated-excel-with-inlinestr-cell-type/). The [test file](http://our.componentone.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/12/TestExcel.xlsx) in that last link will repeat the issue in readxl.

title: Issues with special characters on Windows machine.
description:
Reading a table with names containing special characters something like `"Günther"` results in `"G\xf6tz"` causing problems along the way: E.g. neither grepl() and str_extract() do not work as expected ... 

...  **while something like this works on handwritten data ...**

```
str_extract("G\xfcnther", "ü")
## ü 

str_extract("G\xfcnther", "\xfc")
## "ü"
```

**... it does not work on the data read in by readxl.** My current workaround is to use `iconv(column)` without any further parameters to get values from `"G\xf6tz"` to `"Günther"`. From then on everything works fine. 

My guts tell me, that this is probably one of those R-Windows-Locale-Encoding issues as I use Windows and am used strange happening with characters when read into R.

title: Non-ascii characters in headers in .xls files not read correctly
description:
When the header (the first row) in an .xls file contains non-ASCII characters, it is incorrectly interpreted. For example, an .xls file with this data

```
foo   fooæøå   ☃→☺
bar   bår      test
baz   æz       ☃→☺
```

results in the following (on Windows):

```
> d = read_excel("h:/non-ascii.xls")
> d
  foo fooÃ¦Ã¸Ã¥                â˜ƒâ†’â˜º
1 bar       bår                     test
2 baz        æz <U+2603><U+2192><U+263A>
```

That is, the two _data_ rows are read correctly, but the header row is mangled. It looks like what happens when you interpret UTF-8 byte sequences as ISO-8859-1 (or Windows-1252).

Note that this only happens with .xls files. The same data saved as an .xlsx file works fine.

title: readxl and shiny do not work together
description:
Shiny function  fileInput stores uploaded files in a temp directory without extension. When I try to read the uploaded file with readxl it gives me the error: "Error: Unknown format ."
The same error I am getting when I rename an .xls file removing its extension and trying to read it. 

The workaround is to rename the uploaded file adding the .xls extension back.
file.rename(inFile$datapath, paste(inFile$datapath, ".xlsx", sep=""))

On the topic of detection excel files without extension there is a thread on a mathlab forum that has few working solutions.

title: Missing important information in the documentation: that read_excel returns the tbl object
description:
I understand that tibbles are cool. But they are *not* 100% compatible with data.frames, and the documentation should mention that. 
It is not a minor problem, because the unexpected tibbles can demonstrate their incompatibility after hours of work disguised as `data.frame`, breaking code paths that have already been proven to work. 

It took me more than 5h (five hours!!!) to get to the bottom of this.

Minimal case of the problem. Lets assume that the excel file has only integers inside:
```{r}
library(readxl)
df<-readxl::read_excel(filename) #Returns a data.frame with sneaky little tibble class included... 
indices<-df[,1] #This will be numeric if df is interpreted as data.frame.
df<-df[indices,2] #We simply select needed rows. This works if indices is a numeric.

#Now do some random and innocent computation, like...
#...calling
Hmisc::label

#Now try to run the code again
indices<-df[,1] #This time indices will be a tibble.
df<-df[indices,2] #This line fails miserably, because indices are no longer integers, but one-element list of integers (a tibble).
```

Please observe, that I never imported `tibble`. In fact, I never used it in my life - I usually work with large `data.table`s instead.

description:

It would be helpful if the "n" argument of the xls_col_types function were exposed to the main read_excel function so that I don't have to do the following:

```
my_read_excel <- function(..., n_col_type=100, skip=0) {
  my_col_types <- readxl:::xls_col_types(..., nskip=skip, n=n_col_type)
  read_excel(..., skip=skip, col_types=my_col_types)
}
```

title: Feature request: add parameter for number of rows to read to impute column type
description:
read_excel works fast in part because it imputes col types on first x rows only (is it 100?). The flipside is it doesn't handle sparse columns well (see this SO post: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6099243/read-an-excel-file-directly-from-a-r-script).

It would be helpful to expose this parameter to the user eg 'check_len = 100L', perhaps with '-1' to represent check all rows before assigning column types. [should also be applicable to readr::type_convert]

Supplying coltypes in advance may not be practical in some scenarios (eg when parsing file uploads in a shiny application rather than in interactive use).

My current workaround is to use unexported functions eg xlsx_dim to get number of columns (due to #114,#127), then col_types = rep("text",ncol), then type.convert(as.is = T).

Example use case: reading in market research data, where multiple response questions are often coded as either blank or some text representing the response code rather than T/F and can often contain large tracts of blank rows.

title: Read and write methods that can handle horizontal (row-based) instead of vertical (column-based) data orientation
description:
Would it be possible to introduce read and write methods that can handle Excel data stored in a **horizontal** (row-based) instead of a **vertical** (column-based) orientation (i.e. variables are represented by rows instead of columns) _while preserving the data type/class information_ of the respective variables (i.e. _not_ using coercion to `character` as a "workaround")?

Here's a little example file for both orientations: https://github.com/rappster/stackoverflow/blob/master/excel/row-and-column-based-data.xlsx
- Reading: data would need to be rearranged into a _column-based_ format so it can be stored as a `data.frame`
- Writing: data needs to be rearranged into a _row-based_ format so it complies with the original data orientation

I've elaborated a bit on the motivation for this request in a [stackoverflow post](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/35224338/transposing-a-data-frame-while-preserving-class-data-type-information?noredirect=1#comment58169113_35224338)

While a convincing reason for working against the column-based data orientation standard still escapes me, it seems like a number of platforms/tools in the area of time series analysis/business forecasting are using such a row-based/wide data orientation and I'm going mad trying to deal with it. 

A consideration of this would be greatly appreciated :-)

title: n blank rows in xlsx lead to n trailing NA rows in data frame
description:
Moving from #203, which is about a different problem with blank cells.

Comment I deleted there from @burchill:

> `readxl` gets the initial dimensions of the worksheet, which it thinks **ALWAYS** starts at `A1`, and then goes to whatever the maximum row and column are.  
>
> But `.xlsx` files don't store empty rows, so if the first few rows are entirely empty, `readCols` starts from the first **NON-EMPTY** row, but then still iterates until it gives values for every cell in a matrix of the dimensions it originally measured,   You can replicate it with any simple `.xlsx` file where the data doesn't start until a few rows down.  E.g.:

A | B | C
--|--|--
 | | 
 | | 
 | | 
val1 | val2 | val3
val4 | val5 | val6

becomes:

val1 | val2 | val3
--|--|--
val4 | val5 | val6
`NA` | `NA` | `NA` 
`NA` | `NA` | `NA` 
`NA` | `NA` | `NA`

title: xls files not reading correctly into shiny server pro
description:
I am using `fileInput` to upload a file into a Shiny App in Shiny Server Pro. (Note - I do not have this problem when running the app locally - it only is an issue with Shiny Server Pro.)

I then use `read_excel` to assign the contents of that file to a dataframe object. Finally, I display the data in the dataframe

[hello_world.xlsx](https://github.com/hadley/readxl/files/52051/hello_world.xlsx)

 using `renderDataTable`

This works fine with xls**x** files but not xls files. The issue with the latter is that column headers and character variables do not display.

Here is the `server.R` code:

```
library(shiny)
library(readxl)

shinyServer(function(input, output) {
  current_data <- reactive({
    inFile <- input$file1
    if (is.null(inFile))
      return(NULL)
    file.rename(inFile$datapath,
     paste(inFile$datapath, ".xls", sep="")) #change to xlsx
    current_data <- read_excel(paste(inFile$datapath, ".xls", sep=""), 1, TRUE) #change to xlsx
  })
  output$my_table <- renderDataTable({current_data()})
})
```

and the `ui.R` code:

```

library(shiny)

shinyUI(fluidPage(

  # Application title
  titlePanel("Readxl Test"),

  # Sidebar with a slider input for number of bins
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      fileInput('file1', 'Choose Excel file to upload',#,
        accept = c(".xls",".XLS", ".xlsx")
      )
    ),

    # Show a plot of the generated distribution
    mainPanel(
      dataTableOutput("my_table")

    )
  )
))
```

The files I am reading in are identical save for the extension (and presumably some underlying Excel coding differences between xls and xlsx). I of course modify the code of `server.R` for the change in extension.

I have attached the xlsx files for reference. The xls file is not supported but github but if you open the xlsx and save as xls using Excel you should be able to replicate.

description:
[readxl_example.xlsx](https://github.com/hadley/readxl/files/332860/readxl_example.xlsx)

The problem with the above file is that if you read in a formula, the formula evaluates to 0. At the very least, the formula should evaluate to the formula. For example, the ideal behavior might be the first column reads as text... "=DATE(2015,1,1)".

title: Reads an empty column (NA)
description:
Either when writing to Excel `XLConnect` and/or `openxlsx` or when manipulationg Excel files via the Java API addressed by these packages (necessary when writing formulas), I sometimes seem to end up with a `xlsx` file that has an empty column.

While this certainly is not a good sign (probably still a minor cell offset bug in my code), it surprised me that the "empty" column is only recognized by `readxl::read_excel`, but none of the other functions that will read from `xlsx`.

```
> read_excel(path, sheet = sheet)

1     var_1       asdf       asdf       asdf    NA
2     var_2       asdf       asdf       asdf    NA
3     var_3       asdf       asdf       asdf    NA
4     var_4       asdf       asdf       asdf    NA
