9     var_9       asdf       asdf       asdf    NA
10   var_10       asdf       asdf       asdf    NA
..      ...        ...        ...        ...   ...
```

I've "examplified" one of those files that have an empty column and [uploaded it](https://github.com/rappster/stackoverflow/blob/master/excel/read-performance.xlsx).

Currently, I'm loading the data via `read_excel` and selecting the "valid" data range via the following function as it's still faster than any of the other functions out there (see microbenchmark):

```
ensureNonNaRange <- function(dat) {
  idx_col <- ! dat %>% sapply(function(ii) ii %>% is.na() %>% all())
  idx_row <- ! sapply(1:nrow(dat),
    function(ii) unlist(dat[ii, ]) %>% is.na() %>% all())
  dat[idx_row, idx_col]
}
```

title: Allow user to handle Excel's autoformatting of dates
description:
Excel has aggressive auto-formatting that the user may not have noticed when inputting data. Currently readxl coerces date cells into the raw number used by excel, but usually what I want is the formatted string, as it appears in Excel.

I think that a column with rows that have types that cannot be automatically coerced is a unique to Excel worksheets because of Excel's aggressive auto-formatting. The other tidyverse packages for data import don't have to deal with it, because none of them import data with types that can change across rows (readr doesn't receive type information from the file and haven/feather always receive the same type for a column).

#256 implemented a solution that imported the column as a list type which preserved the type information.

I can also imagine adding a formatting parameter that would give the user control over how a date is formatted when a character column encounters it. I think this would be less flexible, but may make more sense in readxl.

I'm happy to rebase #256 if you are interested, take a stab at implementing the formatting argument, or leave it alone.

title: Support a logical column type?
description:
It seems like an empty column should be filled with logical `NA`s but currently readxl fills with `NA_real_`. I think @hadley has already concurred, at least in principle (https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyverse/issues/34#issuecomment-278500700). Also comes up if all the cells in a column match one of the strings in `na`.

That seems easy enough to do. But it begs the question whether this should be the only way for readxl to return a logical vector. Should `"logical"` become a new column type that can be guessed or that user could specify?

Excel cells can be of Boolean type, so that can be detected when guessing or when enforcing user-specified col types.

But do you take it further? How much effort to make with logical-ish strings and numbers?

title: Converting line breaks in Excel cells
description:
read_excel converts line breaks in Excel cells with the `\r\n` Windows convention.
When printing results, the `\r` causes a non correct location of the cursor in the R Console.
e.g. with the code

```
> cat("this example \r\n continues on the next line")
this example 
 continues on the next line> 
> 
>
>          |
```

the cursor remains placed after `continuous` instead after `>`.
To return to the correct position one has to use Ctrl+L + Enter  or a repeated sequence of Esc.
Using only `\n` the location is correct.

```
> cat("this example \n continues on the next line")
this example 
 continues on the next line> 
> 
> 
> |
```

title: col_types problems
description:
I've run into this issue with read_excel a number of times. I'm reading in a large Excel sheet (60,371 rows and 357 columns). At first I tried to do it without specifying column types. However, some fields with text data had many rows of na values at the top, and were set to numeric by read_excel (I assume it reads some subset of rows at the top before deciding on column types). That resulted in a loss of data when read_excel encountered text data deep in columns that had been set to numeric. The warning() messages read:

In read_xlsx_(path, sheet, col_names = col_names, col_types = col_types,  ... :  [321, 100]: expecting numeric: got 'REDACTED TEXT'

I then set col_types argument with:

`c("text","date","date",rep("text",178),
                                   rep("numeric",176))`

read_excel gave me the error "Error in read_xlsx_(path, sheet, col_names = col_names, col_types = col_types,  : Need one name and type for each column"

I opened the Excel sheet and hit CTL + END to see where Excel thought the end of the data was. The cursor jumped all the way to cell TN60371, which is in line with the last row of data, but 14 columns *past* where the data resides. (I've seen this behavior in Excel many times.)

The data frame produced by read_excel correctly has just 357 columns, so it does somehow weed out those phantom 14 columns recognized by Excel. But my guess is that it applies col_types *before* doing that weeding and therefore doesn't think I've entered the correct number of arguments for col_types.

I tried adding 14 more text columns to the end of my col_types argument, but that didn't work either.

If possible, I think the best solution would be for the col_types argument to be applied after read_excel figures out where the actual data resides in a sheet and how many columns the resulting data frame will have. Also, it seems like the default data type should be text to prevent a loss of data from ever occurring. Or perhaps there could be an option for all columns to be text, without having to specify how many columns there are. The columns can always be converted down the road, of course.

I could probably provide the example file, with dummy values replacing the actual proprietary data, if that would help.

title: Document writing to csv immediately after `read_excel()`
description:
Re: reproducibility.

One of the reasons I think packages like readxl are important is because they allow reading of data as you found it ... even if that's in xls or xlsx.

But I also like to make my workflows transparent, future proof, and version controlled. So I usually save spreadsheet data to plain text form at the same time as I read it into R, just to have a non-binary, plain text snapshot of what the sheet looked like at that moment.

Should `read_excel()` have an argument that applies `readr::write_delim()` to the tibble its returning? Or should I just put sample user code in a vignette or article about using readxl in workflows? The example currently in `excel_sheets()` about [reading all the worksheets at once](http://readxl.tidyverse.org/reference/excel_sheets.html) is another good candidate. And the combination would be great: snapshot a multi-worksheet workbook in a series of csv files.

cc @hadley

title: Behaviour of read_excel na parameter
description:
In the documentation, the `na` parameter of the read_excel function is described as a "Character vector of strings to use for missing values."

This implies that it should be possible to use something like `na = c('NA', 'NA1', 'NA2')` to specify a vector of several strings that represent missing values. Attempting to do this, however, yields:
`Error: expecting a single value`

Examples which include the `na` parameter  show only a single string literal. The documentation should either be altered to something like "A string to use for missing values." to reflect actual behaviour, or (preferably) the code changed to actually allow several missing value strings to be specified.

Anyone who wants to get unique names can easily use tidy_names() function or make.unique and I guess it is safe to assume that if you set col_names to true you named all needed columns to your liking.

title: Leading zeros trimmed when col_type = "text"
description:
I was reading in a series of fixed-digit identification codes that contain leading zeros.  

```
library(readxl)
id_7 <- read_excel(path = "X:/.../id_7.xlsx", 
                   col_names = TRUE, col_types = c("text", "text", "text", "text"), 
                   na = "") 
```
The Excel document I'm reading from has the columns set to a "Custom" number format, where the type is set as 0000000. So in effect Excel pads the id-code with leading zeros until the length of each code is 7 characters. Ideally, this should be read into R (when col_type = "text") as a character vector with the leading zeros included, but unfortunately they are trimmed in the process.

So, to be clear, data that looks like this in your spreadsheet
0000123
0000012
0000001

becomes
123
12
1

in R.

Of course, fixing this in R after the fact is no big deal using stringr::str_pad(), but I figured I'd post the issue anyway as this trimming of leading zeros could lead to some problems for unknowing readxl users.

title: Bug when reading columns with both numeric and text data
description:
Create the following `foo.xls` file:

          A
    1 Employee 
    2 9999999999
    3 a111111111

where the cell:

a) A1 can be any text;
b) A2 can be any number not greater 2147483647;
c) A3 can be any text with at leat one letter.

You get:

    read_xls("foo.xls")
    # # A tibble: 2 × 1
    #     Employee
    #        <chr>
    # 1 -2147483648
    # 2  a111111111

Whatever the number in A2 satisfying the condition b) above, it is always reported as -2147483648.   
One can add more numbers satisfying b) and all will be reported as -2147483648.  
If no cell, apart the header, satisfies c), data is correctly reported.  

`read_xls("foo.xls", col_types='text')` does not fix the problem.  One workaround is:

    x=read_xls("foo.xls", col_types='list')
    x[1]=sapply(x, as.character)


I observed the problem with some files possibly exported from a database and I reproduced the problem with LibreOffice.

title: Feature request: "skip" to accept vector
description:

title: Warning when loading data from Excel spreadsheet if warnPartialMatch options set
description:
I run R with the options **warnPartialMatchArgs**, **warnPartialMatchAttr**, and **warnPartialMatchDollar** set to TRUE, in order to minimize the chances of inadvertently assigning data to the wrong variable. However, this has the effect of generating warnings in cases where, for example, a function in a package calls another function using a partial variable name, or the variable name has been lengthened since the calling function was written.

### Reproducible example

```r
options(warnPartialMatchArgs=TRUE,
        warnPartialMatchAttr=TRUE,
        warnPartialMatchDollar=TRUE)
library(readxl)
datasets <- readxl_example("datasets.xlsx")
test <- read_excel(datasets)
```

On my machine, this results in the following warnings:

```
Warning message:
In read_fun(path = path, sheet = sheet, limits = limits, shim = shim,  :
  partial argument match of 'sheet' to 'sheet_i'
```

### Session Info

```
R version 3.4.4 (2018-03-15)
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)
Running under: Arch Linux

Matrix products: default
BLAS: /usr/lib/libblas.so.3.8.0
LAPACK: /usr/lib/liblapack.so.3.8.0

locale:
 [1] LC_CTYPE=en_US.UTF-8       LC_NUMERIC=C              
 [3] LC_TIME=en_US.UTF-8        LC_COLLATE=en_US.UTF-8    
 [5] LC_MONETARY=en_US.UTF-8    LC_MESSAGES=en_US.UTF-8   
 [7] LC_PAPER=en_US.UTF-8       LC_NAME=C                 
 [9] LC_ADDRESS=C               LC_TELEPHONE=C            
[11] LC_MEASUREMENT=en_US.UTF-8 LC_IDENTIFICATION=C       

attached base packages:
[1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base     

other attached packages:
[1] readxl_1.0.0

loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
[1] compiler_3.4.4   tools_3.4.4      pillar_1.2.1     tibble_1.4.2    
[5] Rcpp_0.12.16     cellranger_1.1.0 rlang_0.2.0     
```

### Possible cause

Digging around in the source a bit, it looks like the function **read_fun()** is being called in **read_excel.R** using the named variable "**sheet**", when it's expecting "**sheet_i**".
I believe you could fix the warning by changing line 145 in **read_excel.R** from:

`read_fun(path = path, sheet = sheet,`

to:

`read_fun(path = path, sheet_i = sheet,`

...but this is my first time looking at the code so I could be wrong about this.

title: Add function to read all sheets into a list
description:
Suggestion:  add a function to read all available sheets into a list.   Simple version below:

```
library(readxl)

read_all_excel<-function(file){
 sheets <- list()
 idx <- 1
 sheet_names <- excel_sheets(file)
 for (s in sheet_names){
  sheets[[idx]] <- read_excel(file, sheet = s)
  idx <- idx + 1
 }
 names(sheets) <- sheet_names
 return(sheets)
}
```

Pros:  
* A convenience for immediately reading in all sheets.

Cons:

title: excel_sheets does not work with *.xltx/*.xltm
description:
### Problem

While `excel_sheets` cannot handle Excel templates (`*.xlt[xm]`), the underlying workhorse `readxl:::xlsx_sheets` can. The error comes from `readxl:::excel_format` which throws an error as soon as the file is not a `*.(xls|xlsx|xlsm)`.

### Possible Fix

Possible fix would be to change `readxl:::excel_format` to:

    function (path) 
    {
        ext <- tolower(tools::file_ext(path))
        switch(ext, xls = "xls", xlsx = "xlsx", xlsm = "xlsx", xltx = "xlsx", xltm = "xlsx", 
            if (nzchar(ext)) {
                stop("Unknown file extension: ", ext, call. = FALSE)
             } else {
                stop("Missing file extension.", call. = FALSE)
            })
    }

There are of course other Excel formats which may deserve to be handled too, Excel 97-2003 templates for instance (`*.xlt`).

### Use Case

If you are wondering, why somebody wants to read in **templates**, let me give you my use case: in a Shiny app I want the user to upload a file containing some data. In order to make sure that the data is compliant with my Shiny app, I do some checks. 

Basically, I compare the structure of the user data with the structure of a template stored in my app folder. This approach avoids hardcoding all the checks. As I am providing an Excel template anyways to the users of my tool, I gain quite some flexibility. I could of course fall back to a `*.xlsx` file, but this does not feel right conceptually.

### Reprex

Sample file:
[Book1.zip](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/1539048/Book1.zip)

    download.file("https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/1539048/Book1.zip", "./Book1.zip")
    unzip("Book1.zip")

    readxl:::excel_sheets("Book1.xltx") 
    # Error: Unknown file extension: xltx

    readxl:::xlsx_sheets("Book1.xltx")
    # [1] "Sheet1"
   
    unlink("Book1.xltx")
    unlink("Book1.zip")

title: Error when a sheet doesn't have a file in /xl/worksheets
description:
One of the Enron files has a sheet, `Module1`, that doesn't have a corresponding file in `/xl/worksheets`.  This causes an error when importing the sheet, e.g. when importing every sheet of every file in a directory.

[daren_farmer__6529__egmnom-Jan.xlsx](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/1505649/daren_farmer__6529__egmnom-Jan.xlsx)

``` r
readxl::excel_sheets("daren_farmer__6529__egmnom-Jan.xlsx")
#> [1] "EGM 60"       "DELV SUMMARY" "EGM 201"      "EGM 202"     
#> [5] "RHODIA"       "Module1"

readxl::read_excel("daren_farmer__6529__egmnom-Jan.xlsx", "Module1")
#> Error in read_fun(path = path, sheet = sheet, limits = limits, shim = shim, : `` not found
```

The problem disappears (for me) when resaving the file with Excel 2010, because Excel creates a file `/xl/worksheets/sheet6.xml`.  So this is presumably rare.

It is named by `excel_sheets()` because it is named in `/xl/workbook.xml`, with an empty `r:id`.  So one way to handle it would be not to include a sheet in `excel_sheets()` if the `r:id` is empty.  Or maybe a graceful failure would be preferable -- I don't really have an opinion.

```xml
<workbook xmlns="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/spreadsheetml/2006/main" xmlns:r="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships" xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006" xmlns:x15="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/spreadsheetml/2010/11/main" mc:Ignorable="x15">
<fileVersion appName="xl" lastEdited="6" lowestEdited="6" rupBuild="14420"/>
<workbookPr codeName="ThisWorkbook" defaultThemeVersion="153222"/>
<mc:AlternateContent xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006">
<mc:Choice Requires="x15">
<x15ac:absPath xmlns:x15ac="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/spreadsheetml/2010/11/ac" url="C:\Users\Felienne\Enron\EnronSpreadsheets\"/>
</mc:Choice>
</mc:AlternateContent>
<bookViews>
<workbookView xWindow="240" yWindow="90" windowWidth="9135" windowHeight="4965" tabRatio="721" activeTab="2"/>
</bookViews>
<sheets>
<sheet name="EGM 60" sheetId="20" r:id="rId1"/>
<sheet name="DELV SUMMARY" sheetId="21" r:id="rId2"/>
<sheet name="EGM 201" sheetId="22" r:id="rId3"/>
<sheet name="EGM 202" sheetId="23" r:id="rId4"/>
<sheet name="RHODIA" sheetId="24" r:id="rId5"/>
<sheet name="Module1" sheetId="19" state="veryHidden" r:id=""/>
</sheets>
<definedNames>
<definedName name="_xlnm.Print_Area" localSheetId="2">'EGM 201'!$A$1:$J$75</definedName>
<definedName name="_xlnm.Print_Area" localSheetId="3">'EGM 202'!$A$1:$D$53</definedName>
<definedName name="_xlnm.Print_Area" localSheetId="0">'EGM 60'!$A$1:$D$34</definedName>
<definedName name="_xlnm.Print_Area" localSheetId="4">RHODIA!$A$1:$D$26</definedName>
</definedNames>
<calcPr calcId="152511" iterate="1" iterateCount="1"/>
</workbook>
```

I don't think the `state="veryHidden"` property is anything to do with it, at least not with modern versions of Excel.  It doesn't prevent there being an `/xl/worksheets/sheet6.xml` file.  The property controls the visibility of the sheet in the Excel UI, and `veryHidden` means it is invisible in both the normal view and the VBA window, and can only be accessed via VBA code (or by unzipping the file).

title: suggestion: tidycols()
description:
This isn't a bug so much as a feature suggestion. One thing that I have noticed when working with Excel workbooks that are provided by non-data colleagues (like marketers, business development, finance people, etc) is that the columns are often named in a very R-unfriendly way, so I wrote a function a while back that automatically converts the column names to snake case and lower-case. Maybe it might be a useful function to add to the package, or to bake into the basic read_excel() function as an argument?

```r
tidycols <- function(df) {
  require(snakecase)
  require(stringr)
  
  dfnames <- colnames(df)
  
  dfnames <- to_snake_case(dfnames,sep_out = "_")
  
  #list some commonly used word separators
  commonseps <- c(' ','.','-','/')
  
  dfnames <- tolower(str_replace_all(dfnames,fixed(commonseps),"_"))
  
  colnames(df) <- dfnames
  
  return(df)
}
```
I've also attached a test file, with several different column name formats, which you can use to test this function:
[test_tidycols.xlsx](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/files/2067139/test_tidycols.xlsx)

title: Don’t trim whitespace by default
description:
This is a request for changing the default `trim_ws` argument from `TRUE` to `FALSE`. Having the default being TRUE leads to *data loss by default*, i.e. the data you get when using `read_excel()` on an Excel is *not* the data that is stored in the file. Having the software trying to be ‘clever’ in second-guessing the content of the data seems to be bad practice. I think having `read_excel()` *not* trim whitespace follows the ‘principle of least surprise’ for users.

I accidently discovered this problem after updating `readxl` to the latest version and an R script I had been using started to produce incorrect result (and it turned out to be caused by stripping whitespace from variable names). Of course, changing the default now will affect people depending on the *new* behaviour, but I think it is better in the long run.

title: feature request: use column names in col_types
description:
Would it be possible to use column names with `col_types` in `read_excel()`? I have some Excel spreadsheets that have many columns, and that need to be formatted with `col_types` because of some badly formatted cells. It gets to a point where it's hard to keep track of what column is what type! For example, I have this snippet of code:

```
obras <- read_excel("CONTROLE DE DOCUMENTOS 2017.xlsx", sheet = "DATAS - ETAPAS",
                 col_types = c("text", "text", "text", "text", "text", 
                               "text", "text", "text", "text", "text", "text", 
                               "text", "text", "text", "text", "text", 
                               "text", "text", "text", "text", "text",
                               "text", "date", "date", "date", "date",
                               "date", "date", "date", "date", "date",
                               "date", "date", "date", "date", "date", 
                               "date", "date", "date", "date", "numeric",

title: Have a way to reveal sheet state (hidden vs visible)
description:
Reading by sheet number, especially when accepting the default of 1, can sometimes read a hidden sheet, which is probably not what the user expects.

readxl should have a way to reveal sheet state, i.e. this information from `xl/workbook.xml`

``` xml
<sheets>
<sheet name="Input" sheetId="1" state="hidden" r:id="rId2"/>
<sheet name="IlluminaSubmissionForm" sheetId="2" state="visible" r:id="rId3"/>
<sheet name="Values" sheetId="3" state="hidden" r:id="rId4"/>
</sheets>
```

That's based on an example from https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/issues/513, where hidden sheets turned out to be the root cause of our confusion.

title: If no col name, fallback to Excel's letter-based column names
description:
When an excel file doesn't have Column Names, the assigned colnames of the df being the same as that of the excel file.
That would also mean that if we're starting from E5 cell, then the returned dataframe's first column name should also be "e".
This way, for instance, when multiple people work on the same excel from a different angle (1 directly and 1 on R), they can easily refer to columns.
> Yo, Gianni... remove column F

---

What happens at the moment

```r
readxl::read_excel(
  "SpreadSheet.xlsx",
  range = cell_limits(c(2, 5), c(NA, NA))
) %>%
  select(-X__2)
```
|x__1|x__3|
|-----|----|
|2     |2    |
|3     |3    |

---

What I suggest:

```r
readxl::read_excel(
  "SpreadSheet.xlsx",
  col_names = FALSE,
  use_excel_col_names = TRUE,
  range = cell_limits(c(2, 5), c(NA, NA))
) %>%
  select(-f)
```
or
```r
readxl::read_excel(
  "SpreadSheet.xlsx",
  col_names = "excel",
  range = cell_limits(c(2, 5), c(NA, NA))
) %>%
  select(-f)
```

|e     |g    |
|-----|----|
|2     |2    |
|3     |3    |

Much easier to understand which columns you're looking at and compare with the excel file.

description:
I found a small issue when reading in an xls file when there is a variable that contains a mixture of characters and strings -- the numbers get filled up with zeros after a decimal point. It seems to work fine for xlsx files but the raw data file I was sent was in the old Excel format and I wanted to read it in directly (whilst testing out the readxl package at the same time!). For example, if I have a dataset looking like:

```
var1
-------
chicken
123
```

The read_excel() function gives the following:

```
library(readxl)
read_excel("Book1.xls")
        var1
1    chicken
2 123.000000

read_excel("Book1.xlsx")
     var1
1 chicken
2     123
```

title: col_names and col_types both explicitly set, but read_excel throws the "need one for each column" error
description:
I have a data set that I'm trying to read, but can't seem to get past this error. Here's my workflow:

``` r
file = "C:/path/to/directory/file.xlsx"
sheet_names <- readxl::excel_sheets(file)
sheet_index <- stringr::str_detect(sheet_names, "^Voice") %>% which() - 1 #index starts at 0

col_names <- .Call("readxl_xlsx_col_names", PACKAGE = "readxl", file, sheet_index, 0)
blank <- sum(col_names == "")
col_names[col_names == ""] <- paste("var", 1:blank, sep = "_")

n <- length(col_names)
col_types <- rep("text", n)

dat <- readxl::read_excel(file, sheet = sheet_index, col_types == col_types, col_names == col_names, skip = 0)
Error: Need one name and type for each column 
```

Here is what col_names and col_types look like:

``` r
> col_names

[46] "var_25"              
> col_types
 [1] "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text" "text"

I thought the missing column names at the end was causing a problem, but that's not it. Then I thought it might be the spacing in the variable names, but that's not it either. So I'm at a total loss as to what to do given that I've explicitly named each variable and declared a type for each as well.

title: Add option to specify file format to support Shiny fileInput()
description: When a file is loaded through a fileInput() widget in a Shiny app, it appears that read_excel scans the file name to determine the file type (at least when input$file[,4] - the file path) is used.  Shiny uploads an extension-less temporary file so read_excel can't open the file.

title: Strings with backslashes
description:
I'm reading in an Excel sheet that has a column of ID numbers like 'S0005497\4'. When this is read into R, I get a double backslash, i.e. 'S0005497\\4'.

Its probably easy enough to remove one of the backslashes but I thought I'd mention this anyway.
